internship.description: A sales support app for easy schedule adjustment with a smartphone
internship.overviewText: During my 2-day internship at Knowledge Work Inc, I participated in a design exploration project centered around the challenge of efficiently scheduling meetings.
internship.scenarioIntro: The project was inspired by the following hypothetical scenario, provided by the company:
internship.scenarioBullet1: {A} needed a new meeting time after the first consultation.
internship.scenarioBullet4: Before proposing times to {C} and {D}, {A} confirmed availability with {B}.
internship.scenarioBullet5: {A} then presented the options to {C} and {D}.
internship.scenarioBullet6: {C} coordinated with {D} for a common time.
internship.scenarioBullet8: Finally, {C} provided a mutually agreed time to {A}.
internship.role: As a UI/UX design intern, my role involved conducting user research, creating wireframes, designing user interfaces...
internship.designProcessText: The design process involved a combination of research, prototyping, and testing.
internship.infoGathering: I began by reviewing existing scheduling apps, and conducting competitive analysis. This research helped me identify key user needs and pain points.
internship.prototyping: After the research, I created low-fidelity wireframes from selecting candidate date and time to requesting them for the companion. I then conducted usability testing with a sales person at the company I participated.
internship.improvements: Based on the results of our usability testing, I made several key improvements to the design, including the fact that travel time needs to be considered as well as available slots, and adding clearer instructions. These improvements significantly enhanced the overall user experience.
internship.conditionSearchText: Search by "Refine by criteria" at the top of the calendar view (companion / business target / location / duration)
internship.searchResultsText1: The "Search results" view dims the surrounding area, highlighting the specified period (from the 5th to the 9th). Results are presented in a list view at the bottom on the page, and users can easily adjust the time by tapping the right arrow.
internship.searchResultsText2: In Day view of the calendar, the meeting time and the travel time displayed, eliminating the need to worry about travel time.
internship.sendRequestText: The screen transitions to the confirmation page about the detail.
internship.impressionsPoint1: The most impressive part was interviewing the sales staff and receiving valuable feedback on the designs at that point in time.
internship.impressionsPoint2: The reactions of the designers during the presentation were impressive; they took the students' work seriously and reacted with large nods of their heads.
internship.impressionsPoint3: Feedback was provided in the form of a set of good points (GOOD), opportunities for improvement (OPPORTUNITY) and areas for improvement (IMPROVE).
internship.reflectionPoint1: As mentioned above, I got an opportunity to interview a sales person and his feedback provided me with more practical design ideas. For me, the interview was my first experience and very valuable.
internship.reflectionPoint2: I received realistic advice for improvement that I need to consider not only available slots but also travel time. I learned not only to consider the usability and usability of the application, but also the perspective of what users want to use this application in what environment and for what purpose.
internship.reflectionPoint3: As for the function to obtain location information of each individual, I felt that privacy concerns and the fact that some people register locations in their calendars while others do not, were challenges in connecting design with the real world.

gymDashboard.overviewText: My 24-hour gym had unpredictable crowd conditions, making it impossible to plan efficient training schedules. Particularly during evening hours, long wait times prevented effective use of limited exercise time. This project built a system that optimizes gym usage through a data-driven approach.
gymDashboard.challengesIntro: This project built a distributed system integrating 4 platforms (iOS, iCloud, GitHub Actions, Vercel) and tackled the following technical challenges:
gymDashboard.dataCollectionSemiAuto: Data Collection Semi-Automation: From screenshot acquisition to iCloud sync under iOS constraints
gymDashboard.ocrAccuracyImprovement: OCR Accuracy Improvement: Achieved 80% OCR processing success rate through image preprocessing
gymDashboard.cicdIntegration: CI/CD Integration: Fully automated pipeline with GitHub Actions
gymDashboard.dataVisualization: Data Visualization: Interactive dashboard with Next.js + Chart.js
gymDashboard.operationOptimization: Operation Optimization: Robust infrastructure achieving 99.1% uptime
gymDashboard.roleDescription: I was consistently responsible for the entire system architecture design, implementation, and operation, demonstrating practical skills in creative problem-solving under constrained environments and integration of multiple technical domains.
gymDashboard.systemFlowDescription: The diagram is the visualization for the flow of this project:
gymDashboard.ocrSuccessRate: OCR Processing Success Rate: 80% (Tesseract + OpenCV preprocessing)
gymDashboard.designProcessText: In designing a complex system that integrates multiple technical domains, I adopted a phased approach. I proceeded systematically from personal problem-solving through understanding technical constraints to implementation.
gymDashboard.designStep1Body: Analysis of gym user behavior patterns and identification of pain points. Investigation of technical constraints (iOS automation limitations, OCR accuracy constraints) and feasibility assessment.
gymDashboard.designStep2Body: Distributed system design for iOS → iCloud → GitHub Actions → Vercel. End-to-end design from screenshot acquisition to dashboard display.
gymDashboard.designStep3Body: OCR accuracy optimization through image preprocessing. Resolution of synchronization issues between 4 platforms and UX optimization.
gymDashboard.dataCollectionText1: My gym's dedicated app is only accessible through a closed iOS app with no web version, making complete automation technically impossible. Therefore, I designed a "context-aware semi-automation" system that achieved sustainable data collection integrated into my natural behavior flow.
gymDashboard.dataCollectionText2: Initially, I configured Apple Shortcut to perform OCR within Automation and extract time, number of people, and crowd labels, but text corruption and unwanted text extraction occurred. Therefore, I changed the design to specialize Apple Shortcut for screenshot capturing and saving to iCloud Drive with datetime filenames, while performing OCR processing on the GitHub Actions side.
gymDashboard.alertInitialDesignDescription: OCR performed within Apple Shortcut, causing text corruption and unwanted text extraction
gymDashboard.alertOptimizedDesignDescription: Apple Shortcut specialized for screenshot capture and iCloud saving, OCR processing moved to GitHub Actions
gymDashboard.ocrText1: I learned that image preprocessing is more important than expected for OCR accuracy improvement. Initially, I performed OCR processing within Apple Shortcut, but text corruption and unwanted text extraction occurred, so I moved the processing to the GitHub Actions side.
gymDashboard.ocrText2: I implemented 3-stage image preprocessing using OpenCV:
gymDashboard.ocrStep1: Grayscale Conversion (cv2.cvtColor) - Convert color images to a more processable format
gymDashboard.ocrStep2: Noise Removal (cv2.fastNlMeansDenoising) - Effectively remove image noise
gymDashboard.ocrStep3: Adaptive Contrast Enhancement (cv2.createCLAHE) - Clarify character outlines
gymDashboard.ocrText3Middle: as the main engine with Japanese and English support (jpn+eng), and
gymDashboard.ocrText3After: is disabled for performance optimization. I have accumulated 354 data points and built a stable data collection pipeline.
gymDashboard.githubActionsSuccess: After 7 failures with GitHub Actions, I achieved initial success on the 8th attempt.
gymDashboard.failureCausesProcess: The main failure causes and resolution process are as follows.
gymDashboard.decisiveFixTextMiddle: package was deprecated in Ubuntu 24.04 environment with a single change to
gymDashboard.syncStep2: Local side: launchd script Git integration fix
gymDashboard.syncResult: This enabled the hybrid system (local iCloud sync + GitHub Actions processing) to work properly, achieving 99.1% uptime.
gymDashboard.learningText1: Through this project, I experienced the joy of solving small daily problems with technology. While I initially aimed for complete automation, finding the "right level of automation" with manual operation when launching the gym app was a significant learning.
gymDashboard.learningText2: Technically, I faced an unexpected challenge where BOT commits from GitHub Actions do not trigger Vercel's automatic deployment. In solving this problem, I gained deep understanding of CI/CD pipeline mechanisms and inter-service coordination.
gymDashboard.prospectsText: Currently, data acquisition timing is unstable as it depends on when I remember to do it, so I haven't achieved regular and stable data collection like acquiring data at 0 minutes of every hour. I expect that future AI developments will enable Siri to operate apps, or Shortcuts will evolve to allow more advanced configurations, making more complete automation possible.

tldr.title: TL;DR

tldr.solutionText: Automated data pipeline with 80% OCR accuracy and 99.1% uptime.

ukiyoe.title: Ukiyoe: Layer by Layer
ukiyoe.subtitle: Experiencing the evolution of woodblock printing through interactive animation
ukiyoe.overviewText1: A couple of years ago, I visited the ukiyoe gallery at the Tokyo National Museum. I had seen woodblock prints in textbooks, but the real thing was different. Observing the texture of the paper and the depth of the pigments up close, seeing snow falling on Shinagawa and Fuji rising beyond low rooftops, I felt a quiet resonance with the same Tokyo seen through the eyes and craft of people who lived here centuries ago. Now that AI tools have matured enough to support complex front-end projects, I saw a chance to recreate the layered printing process as an interactive web experience.
ukiyoe.overviewText2: I visualized the evolution of printing techniques from monochrome sumizuri-e to full-color nishiki-e through scroll-driven animations. Color layers stack one by one, just as a printer would have done by hand, recreating the printing process.
ukiyoe.researchIntro: Before writing a single line of code, I immersed myself in the world of ukiyoe, studying printing techniques, analyzing color palettes, and understanding centuries of cultural context.
ukiyoe.culturalResearchText: I studied over 25 reference sites including museum archives, printmaking workshops, and academic resources. This research covered the complete woodblock printing process, from carving woodblocks to applying pigments, aligning registration marks (kento), and the sequential layering of colors. Understanding this process was essential to designing animations that authentically represent how each print was made.
ukiyoe.colorAnalysisText: Using Python scripts, I extracted dominant color palettes from actual ukiyoe prints across different eras. This analysis revealed how the available pigment range expanded over time, from pure black ink in sumizuri-e to the rich, multi-layered palette of nishiki-e. These extracted colors became the foundation of the site's design system, with CSS variables mapped to historically accurate pigments.
ukiyoe.printingProcessText: In nishiki-e, a single print could require 10 or more separate woodblocks, each carrying a different color. Understanding this precise sequence was crucial for designing layer-stacking animations where each color appears in historically accurate order.
ukiyoe.designProcessIntro: From the trial and error of visual language and motifs to interactive visualizations of historical color data, each process went through its own cycle of exploration, testing, and refinement.
ukiyoe.topPageDesignHeroAlt: Collage of the top page design history
ukiyoe.topPageDesignHeroCaption: A collage-style visual bringing together the design history of the top page.
ukiyoe.topPageDesignText1: The core concept was to let you, the user, experience how a woodblock print comes together, layer by layer. I began by separating actual ukiyoe prints into individual color layers using Adobe Fresco, hand-painting each layer to match the original pigment colors. This was one of the most labor-intensive parts of the project; AI tools at the time could not generate these layers with the necessary precision.
ukiyoe.topPageDesignText2: I then converted these layers into SVG format. On the site's top page, I arranged them in an isometric perspective inspired by the flattened spatial composition characteristic of Japanese painting. I explored multiple approaches, from simple vertical stacking to a media-player-style timeline control, before settling on scroll-driven isometric animation.
ukiyoe.topPageDesignText3: A key design challenge was storytelling. Raw layer animations without context would confuse first-time visitors. I iterated on the accompanying text sections, balancing educational depth with visual clarity.
ukiyoe.timelineDesignText1: The timeline page went through a fundamental architectural shift. Initial designs used a horizontal scroll mechanism with wheel event capture, but this conflicted with native scrolling behavior and caused persistent UX issues. After two failed patch attempts, I rebuilt the entire page using native vertical scroll with parallax effects.
ukiyoe.timelineDesignText2: The key design insight came from considering how ukiyoe was consumed in the Edo period: not in museum frames, but as mass-produced prints in everyday life. This led to a more organic, randomized artwork layout rather than a rigid grid, with each era's artworks presented alongside a color swatch visualization showing how the available palette expanded over time.
ukiyoe.motifsIntro:
Kushi-dango are three-colored rice dumplings on a skewer (pink, white, and green), a traditional Japanese sweet enjoyed at tea houses and during hanami and tsukimi since the Edo period. The shape of round mochi threaded on a stick inspired this site's recurring navigation pattern: the line-and-dot motif across timeline bars, CTAs, and indicators.

On the timeline page, white circular indicators against the dark background serve as a double metaphor: dango on a skewer, and the moon as ukiyoe artists often depicted it, a luminous white circle. Moon viewing (tsukimi) and dango are culturally inseparable in Japan; offerings of dango are placed beneath the harvest moon on the fifteenth night.

The right column shows that dango was a recurring subject in ukiyoe itself, appearing in scenes of tea houses, street vendors, and seasonal customs. It shows how deeply this confection was embedded in Edo-period visual culture.
ukiyoe.motifsFigma: The motif first took shape during the top page design (Phase 3) in Figma, where the layer was literally named "Dango." What began as a playful visual accent for the timeline section evolved into a unifying design element across the entire project.
ukiyoe.motifsSpread: The kushi-dango pattern appears in four distinct forms: the timeline date bar (a horizontal line ending in a dot), the "Explore the history of ukiyo-e" CTA (a line with a ringed dot that pulses on hover), the vertical dot navigation (a skewer line threading through circular indicators), and the Dawn page gallery indicators. Each instance adapts the same line-through-circles concept to its context while maintaining visual consistency.
ukiyoe.colorSystemIntro: The timeline gallery features a color proportion bar for each historical period, showing how the available pigment palette expanded over centuries. But how were these ratios determined?
ukiyoe.colorSystemMethod: Rather than pixel-level analysis of artworks, the proportions are estimated from art historical knowledge. The technique descriptions for each era guided the weighting. For sumizuri-e (ink-only prints), black ink dominates at 50-60%. For benizuri-e, red and green emerge as the technique's defining colors. By the nishiki-e era, colors distribute more evenly as multi-block printing allowed a full spectrum. The values are hand-curated estimates, documented with their reasoning and limitations.
ukiyoe.colorSystemViz: In the timeline gallery, each era displays a horizontal bar where the width of each color segment equals its estimated proportion. Nine canonical color slots, from sumi (ink black) to bero (Prussian blue), are normalized so that active colors are prominent while unused slots appear as ghost elements. This visualization communicates at a glance how printmaking evolved from monochrome to polychrome.
ukiyoe.logoDesignText1: The first version, a kaleidoscope of repeated faces, looked decorative but didn't actually capture what makes ukiyo-e ukiyo-e, so I went back to research. Asking an AI model to summarize ukiyo-e's compositional grammar, then checking the answer against real prints, turned up four traits that kept recurring: bold foreground cropping, diagonal dynamism, an unconventional mixed-perspective deformation, and a deliberate awareness of the frame and negative space. This is the same visual logic later inherited by the Impressionists.
ukiyoe.logoDesignText2: The mark applies the first of those traits directly: instead of centering the main shape, it's cropped in close and pushed off-axis, the way a print crops a bridge or a branch until it runs off the frame. Inside a hanko-style double-square seal, a circle, a diagonal cut, and a small offset window interlock without ever overlapping: one line, one pass, one impression. It isn't a portrait of any single print; it's the printing logic itself, reduced to a mark small enough for a favicon and legible enough for a full page.
ukiyoe.handColoringText1: The core animation on this site shows color layers stacking to form a complete print, just as a real Edo-period printer would have pressed each woodblock in sequence. To build this, I needed images of each individual color layer: the red pigment areas on one layer, green foliage on another, gold accents on a third.
ukiyoe.handColoringText2: These assets do not exist in any dataset. I tried AI image generation, but it could not produce layers with the color accuracy and edge precision required to align and stack convincingly. So I did what a printer would have done: I separated the colors by hand.
ukiyoe.handColoringText3: Using Adobe Fresco, I painted each layer individually, referencing the original prints to match pigment areas. This was the most time-consuming part of the entire project, and the part AI could not shortcut. The timelapse below shows the process.
ukiyoe.captionHandColoring: Timelapse of hand-painting individual color layers in Adobe Fresco. Each pigment separated by hand to recreate the woodblock printing process.
ukiyoe.aiCraftTitle: AI Can Create, But It Can't Craft
ukiyoe.aiCraftText1: I estimated this project would take 2 to 3 weeks with AI handling the implementation. It took three months. Not because AI failed, but because the work that mattered most turned out to be the work AI could not do: hand-coloring layer assets, making cultural design judgments, and finding unexpected connections between historical research and interaction design.
ukiyoe.aiCraftText2: AI was still central to execution. I used Claude and Cursor to prototype components, iterate on responsive layouts, and implement scroll-driven animations that would have taken much longer to build alone. But my process goes beyond prompting. I bring cultural context, historical references, and design intent into every interaction. When building the timeline's color system, I did not ask AI to "pick nice colors." I researched pigment histories, wrote Python scripts to extract colors from museum archives, then designed a canonical slot structure that makes 130 years of palette evolution legible at a glance. AI implemented each step faster. The story, the structure, and the judgment were mine.
ukiyoe.aiCraftText3: AI can create, but it can't craft. Craft is the narrative behind a design choice, the sensitivity to a cultural context, the attention to a detail that nobody requested but that makes the whole thing feel intentional. The isometric layer animations, the kushi-dango navigation motif, the canonical color slots: each reflects a specific design decision rooted in genuine research, not generic output. What AI gave me was speed. What I brought was direction, a cultural story, and the conviction that the details matter.
ukiyoe.technicalIntro: Built as a custom design system of CSS variables carrying historically-derived color tokens, with scroll-driven animation throughout.
ukiyoe.techFeature1Text: Layer-stacking animations are driven directly by scroll position. Each technique era has its own set of hand-painted layers that stack progressively.
ukiyoe.techFeature2Text: A native scroll-based parallax system where artwork images move at different speeds based on depth. Fixed period panels and progress indicators help users navigate five historical eras.
ukiyoe.techFeature3Text: CSS variables map traditional color names like sumi-iro (ink black), beni-iro (crimson), and ai-iro (indigo), creating a cohesive visual language that respects the source material.
ukiyoe.techFeature4Text: Nine normalized color slots per era: active colors displayed prominently, unused slots as ghost elements. This visually communicates how the printmaking palette expanded from monochrome to polychrome.
ukiyoe.aiRoleText1: AI accelerated ideation and code implementation, but could not create the hand-painted layer assets or make nuanced cultural design judgments. The most valuable outcomes came from human curiosity: the leap from studying printing processes to imagining isometric layer animations, and the decision to use historically extracted colors rather than approximated palettes.
ukiyoe.aiRoleText2: The most valuable outcomes came from human curiosity: the leap from studying printing processes to imagining isometric layer animations, the insight that ukiyoe was folk art rather than museum art, and the decision to use historically extracted colors rather than approximated palettes. AI was a powerful collaborator, but the creative direction required human exploration.
ukiyoe.learningsText1: Standing in front of those prints at the Tokyo National Museum, I was moved by a simple fact: the same streets I walk today once looked entirely different, and someone centuries ago cared enough to carve that vision into wood, ink it, and press it onto paper, one color at a time. This project let me follow that same impulse through a different medium.
ukiyoe.learningsText2: What I learned is that genuine curiosity about a subject is not separate from the design process. It is the design process. Understanding that nishiki-e required 10+ woodblocks shaped the animation sequence. Knowing that ukiyoe was mass-produced popular art, not gallery pieces, shaped the timeline's casual layout. Researching Edo-period publisher marks shaped the logo. Every design decision traced back to something I learned because I wanted to, not because a brief required it.
ukiyoe.learningsText3: Cultural context is not decoration. It is the design foundation. And in an era where AI can generate layouts, write code, and produce visual assets at speed, what sets work apart is craft: the cultural story behind each decision, the hand-painted layers that no algorithm could shortcut, and the conviction that these details are what make a project feel genuinely made, not just generated.
ukiyoe.futureText: Ongoing optimization for mobile performance and image loading, with future plans for additional artwork data, audio narration, and deeper interactive demonstrations of individual printing techniques.
ukiyoe.captionResearch: Research across 25+ museum archives, printmaking workshops, and academic sources. This led to a fundamental understanding of the complete woodblock process, from carving to sequential color layering.
ukiyoe.captionColorAnalysis: Python-extracted color palettes from actual prints across eras, from pure black ink in sumizuri-e to the rich, multi-layered spectrum of nishiki-e.
ukiyoe.captionTopPage: Hand-painted layers separated in Adobe Fresco, arranged in isometric perspective. Multiple approaches explored before settling on scroll-driven animation.
ukiyoe.captionTimeline: Rebuilt from horizontal scroll to native vertical scroll with parallax, inspired by how ukiyoe was consumed as everyday mass-produced prints, not museum pieces.
ukiyoe.captionMotifs: Left to right: Timeline UI navigation with dango-inspired indicators; AI-generated photorealistic kushi-dango; ukiyoe depicting dango in everyday Edo life. Artworks: Utagawa Kuniyoshi, Dango Shop at the Rabbit Festival (卯のだんごや); Suzuki Harunobu, Kasamori Osen Holding Dango (団子を持つ笠森お仙); Kachōrō Kunisada, Famous Places of the Eastern Capital: Takanawa in the Eighth Month (東都名所遊覧 葉月高輪).
ukiyoe.captionColorSystem: Color proportions estimated from art historical knowledge, showing how the printmaking palette expanded from monochrome to polychrome across centuries.
ukiyoe.captionLogo: From a kaleidoscope that looked pretty but said nothing, through researching ukiyo-e's actual compositional grammar, to a seal mark built on bold cropping and off-center placement.

figmaPlugins.title: Figma Plugins & Widgets
figmaPlugins.subtitle: Tools born from dialogue with AI
figmaPlugins.overviewText1: As a designer embedded in a large-scale design system project, I kept encountering repetitive tasks and workflow gaps that no existing plugin addressed. Rather than waiting for someone else to solve them, I started building my own, using AI as a coding partner through vibe-coding sessions with Claude and Cursor.
figmaPlugins.overviewText2: What began as quick personal utilities grew into an ecosystem of plugins and widgets spanning personal tools and enterprise design system infrastructure. Each one was born from a real problem, shaped through iterative dialogue with AI, and refined against actual daily use.
figmaPlugins.heroTitle: Tools born from dialogue with AI
figmaPlugins.heroDescription: An ecosystem of interconnected tools: personal utilities and enterprise design system infrastructure, all cultivated through AI collaboration.

airlineDesignSystem.title: Airline Design System
airlineDesignSystem.subtitle: A comprehensive design system unifying 9 digital platforms, from design tokens and custom Figma plugins to production-ready React components.
airlineDesignSystem.overviewText1: A major airline operates 9 digital platforms: 2 mobile apps and 7 web variants across languages and regions. Each had evolved independently, resulting in visual inconsistencies, duplicated components, and mounting design debt that slowed every team working on the product.
airlineDesignSystem.overviewText2: I was brought in as the sole design system designer and developer to build a unified design language from the ground up. Guided by Dan Mall's "Design That Scales" methodology, I focused not just on creating a token system and component library, but on making the system so useful that adoption became the path of least resistance.
airlineDesignSystem.challenge1: Visual inconsistency across 9 platforms (2 apps, 7 web variants) with no shared design language
airlineDesignSystem.challenge2: Need to support both iOS Human Interface Guidelines and Android Material Design 3 from a single source of truth
airlineDesignSystem.challenge3: Legacy design files with unbound values, manual workflows, and no token architecture in place
airlineDesignSystem.roleText: I was the sole designer and developer on the design system, responsible for token architecture, component audit, Figma plugin development, frontend prototype implementation, and documentation. I worked as part of Accenture Song, collaborating with the airline's internal design and development teams.
airlineDesignSystem.captionRoadmap: 4-phase project roadmap spanning research, token design, component implementation, and documentation
airlineDesignSystem.designProcessIntro: The design process balanced deep research with rapid prototyping. I needed to understand the existing landscape before proposing a system, then validate architectural decisions through working code.
airlineDesignSystem.competitiveText: I audited 12 airline and transportation websites (Alaska Airlines, Korean Air, Qantas, SNCF, SBB, Deutsche Bahn, and more) to understand industry patterns for booking flows, navigation, and component usage. This research informed our token naming conventions, spacing scale, and component priority matrix.
airlineDesignSystem.captionCompetitive: Competitive audit across 12 airline and transportation websites, analyzing booking flows, navigation patterns, and component systems
airlineDesignSystem.auditText: I systematically audited all 9 platforms, identifying 53 unique UI components across 6 categories: Input (16), Navigation (13), Display (9), Feedback (4), Layout (10), and Icons (1). Each component was mapped against the platforms where it appeared, revealing where inconsistencies were most severe and where standardization would have the highest impact.
airlineDesignSystem.tokenText: I designed a two-layer token system. Primitive tokens define the raw palette (colors, spacing, typography values), while Semantic tokens assign meaning (primary, surface, on-surface). This separation means a brand refresh only requires updating the Primitive layer, with all Semantic references updating automatically. I referenced Serendie, Material Design, and Atlassian's systems in designing this architecture.
airlineDesignSystem.captionToken: Two-layer token architecture: Primitive (raw values) mapped to Semantic (role-based) tokens
airlineDesignSystem.colorTypoText: The color system follows Material Design 3's tonal palette approach with 80 primitive colors and 59 semantic tokens, all WCAG AA compliant. Three color modes (Light, Dark, GraySwitch) ensure flexibility across contexts. Typography uses 25 styles based on MD3's type roles (display, headline, title, body, label), with 3 platform modes (Web, iOS, Android) that adjust sizes and weights for each rendering environment.
airlineDesignSystem.solutionIntro: The design system shipped as four interconnected deliverables: a token system, custom Figma plugins, a component prototype, and comprehensive documentation.
airlineDesignSystem.tokenSystemText: The token system is organized into 6 Figma Variable collections covering color, typography, spacing, border radius, shadows, and component-specific values. Together they contain 399 variables supporting 3 color modes and 3 typography modes.
airlineDesignSystem.pluginsText: To make the design system practical rather than theoretical, I built custom Figma plugins that automate the most tedious parts of design system work. Each plugin solves a specific workflow bottleneck, from initial token setup to ongoing production support.
airlineDesignSystem.prototypeText: I built a living prototype in code, on top of an existing component base. The prototype serves as both a reference implementation and a testing ground for token values. It includes 11 page variants demonstrating Button, TextField, Assist Chip, Header, Navigation, and Loading components, all themed with the airline's brand tokens.
airlineDesignSystem.docsText: I authored 51+ markdown documents organized into 5 categories: reference materials, analysis (UI audits, gap analysis, brand investigation), design specifications (component specs, typography, color), implementation guides, and planning documents. This documentation ensures the system can be maintained and extended by future designers and developers.
airlineDesignSystem.impactText: The design system established a unified visual foundation across 9 digital platforms for the first time. Developers can now reference a single token source for colors, typography, and spacing, eliminating the per-platform style drift that had accumulated over years. The custom Figma plugins reduced what had been manual, error-prone token setup to automated, repeatable workflows.
airlineDesignSystem.learningText: The most important lesson came from Dan Mall's framework: "Build it and they will come" doesn't work for design systems. Adoption requires making the system the path of least resistance. The Figma plugins were crucial here: they didn't just automate tasks, they made following the design system easier than not following it. The Variable Migrator plugin, for example, let designers update legacy files to the new token system in minutes rather than days.
airlineDesignSystem.technicalText: Building custom Figma plugins taught me that the gap between design and development is often a tooling problem, not a communication problem. When designers have plugins that enforce token usage and developers have a Next.js prototype showing exactly how components should render, alignment happens naturally. I'd like to explore deeper Code Connect integration and automated design-to-code pipelines in future projects.

nakahatsu.title: Nakahatsu Shoten Website
nakahatsu.subtitle: A Kanazawa soy sauce and miso maker's company site and shop, rebuilt as one Shopify store
nakahatsu.overviewText1: Nakahatsu Shoten (株式会社中初商店) makes soy sauce and miso in Kanazawa. It was founded in 1896 as a food retailer and later moved into brewing. Online, the business ran two separate systems: a WordPress site for the company and an EC-CUBE shop. The designs and navigation did not match, and updates had to be made in two places.
nakahatsu.overviewText2: I took the project on as an individual, through an introduction from an acquaintance. This phase is a domestic shop shown in Japanese, English and French. Selling overseas is outside the scope.
nakahatsu.overviewText2Live: I took the project on as an individual, through an introduction from an acquaintance. It is a domestic shop shown in Japanese, English and French. Selling overseas is outside the scope.
nakahatsu.challenge1: The shop could not take credit cards. The only ways to pay were bank transfer, postal transfer and cash on delivery.
nakahatsu.challenge2: The site was in Japanese only, with no official translation. A visitor who could not read Japanese had to rely on the browser's machine translation, with no guarantee that the product and purchasing information would come across as intended. Prices were in yen only.
nakahatsu.challenge3: When I tried it in the first month, the confirmation email for a new account took about two hours to arrive. Registering again in the meantime showed "This email address cannot be used".
nakahatsu.challenge4: The purchase path was split between WordPress and the shop. The designs could not be unified, and updates had to be done twice.
nakahatsu.challenge5: What buyers want to know before purchase, such as shipping fees, payment methods and returns, was only partly written on the legal notice page, and not where customers would naturally look.
nakahatsu.contextText: In the first month of the project I looked at ten sites in Japan, including some in Ishikawa, that sell soy sauce, miso and other fermented foods online. I prioritised companies more than a hundred years old and chose sites strong in design, storytelling or usability. I later checked each one again, looking at the top page, header and footer, and found none that shows its shop in more than one language. The ten sites are listed at the foot of this page.
nakahatsu.roleText: I took this on as an individual, through an introduction from an acquaintance, and I was the only person on the project. The client is a company, and I have dealt directly with the family who run it since the first proposal.
nakahatsu.scope1: Proposal and estimate, based on a survey of the existing site
nakahatsu.scope2: Research, requirements, and UI design in Figma for desktop and mobile
nakahatsu.scope3: Design system, with color and spacing values kept the same in Figma and in code
nakahatsu.scope4: Shopify implementation: customizing an existing theme, migrating products, and setting up shipping and checkout
nakahatsu.scope5: Japanese, English and French display (the contract covers Japanese and English; the client asked for French to be added)
nakahatsu.scope6: Client coordination: meetings, written requests, reviews, and revisions
nakahatsu.scopeNote: Enabling payments, moving the domain and registering six more products are steps only the client can take, so they remain with the client.
nakahatsu.captionBeforeAfter: Before: the top page of the WordPress company site. After: the new top page. The shop was a separate system (EC-CUBE).
nakahatsu.designProcessIntro: In March we agreed to keep the existing design and skip wireframes. After that I proposed a redesign, and because the first version I showed was received well, I moved on to a full redesign.
nakahatsu.researchText: Besides the ten similar sites, I looked at the history pages of six long-established companies, the geography and history of the neighborhood, and three moodboard directions. What I found was that the company's history from 1896, the origin of its name and its sense of place existed only as text on the site.
nakahatsu.twoDirectionsTitle: Showing two versions side by side
nakahatsu.twoDirectionsText: Because we had agreed to keep the existing design, I made two versions: v1 reproduced the existing site and v2 was the redesign. When I shared them side by side, the client replied that v2 was easy to see, with a clean structure that included the purchase path (summarised). After that I worked mainly on v2.
nakahatsu.aboutText: The version in the store now is not the one from August. The changes are on both the home page and the About page, and the About page changed the most. For the home page's "About Nakahatsu Shoten" block I laid out several options, and the client chose the one with three tall photographs of the building. On the About page I rebuilt the two brewing sections, tenyu soy sauce and tenyu miso, with the body text laid over a photograph. When the screen is wide enough the Japanese text runs vertically, and English and French stay horizontal.
nakahatsu.motionText: The "Oidemashi" heading (a Kanazawa way of saying welcome) starts with a small round photograph of the two people who make the products, which grows and becomes a rectangle. I made it to introduce them, who are special to this shop, quietly and gracefully. For visitors who ask for reduced motion, and when scripts are off, it is shown as a rectangle from the start.
nakahatsu.dsText: I built a design system first, covering colors, spacing, type styles and shared parts, and assembled the screens from it. When the values in Figma and in code drift apart, I look at the site to fix something and find that Figma no longer matches it. So a script keeps the color and spacing values the same in both.
nakahatsu.captionBilingual: The same hero in Japanese and in English.
nakahatsu.solutionIntro: The result is one Shopify store that covers the whole site. I started from an existing Shopify theme and made the layout and sections for this site.
nakahatsu.buildText: The pages are the home page, product, collection, search, About, contact, the news list and articles, FAQ, 404, policies and customer accounts. The twelve products and the shipping table were migrated from the old site. I grouped the shipping rates into ten zones from the old table, and the client agreed to them. Sign-in works with Shopify accounts as well as Google and Facebook (Meta). I issued a client ID and a client secret for each, set them in Shopify's customer account settings, and tested the sign-in.
nakahatsu.captionProducts: Part of the product list. The products were migrated from the old site.
nakahatsu.captionResponsive: The home page at 1440 and 390 pixels, drawn at the same scale. The vertical copy stays in place on both.
nakahatsu.checkoutText: The brand color is enji, a deep crimson. It is one of the Kaga Gosai, the five traditional colors of Kanazawa, so it is rooted in this place. I had used it in checkout as well, but there the links are drawn as underlined text in the same color, and in crimson they did not read as links. So I split it: crimson up to the cart, and Shopify's standard blue (#005BD3) from checkout onward. Showing the brand and making purchase easy to follow pull in different directions, and I chose to draw that line on purpose.
nakahatsu.qualityText: I checked the work in several rounds. First, a review found 43 issues (10 high, 19 medium, 14 low), and I fixed the high-severity ones that the theme could fix. I checked the 13 English pages and no Japanese text was left. After that, a separate AI agent, not the one that made the changes, checked 204 screens, and I fixed what it found (3 critical, 9 major, 20 minor).
nakahatsu.qualityTextLive: I checked the work in several rounds. In May 2026 a review found 43 issues (10 high, 19 medium, 14 low), and I fixed the high-severity ones that the theme could fix. On May 16 I checked the 13 English pages and no Japanese text was left. On October 18 and 19 a separate AI agent, not the one that made the changes, checked 204 screens, and I fixed what it found (3 critical, 9 major, 20 minor).
nakahatsu.statusText: The project is still in progress. The store runs on a password-protected theme and has not launched, and it has not been through the client's acceptance. What remains is on the client side. Because the site has not launched, there are no sales, conversion, or traffic figures yet. I will add them when there are.
nakahatsu.aiLeverageTitle: What only became possible with AI
nakahatsu.aiLeverageText: Shopify was a platform I had never touched before this project. I could not have carried it this far as one person without AI assistance. Working in a technology you are new to, and keeping the tasks moving, are two of the places where AI helps most.
nakahatsu.aiLimitTitle: What AI could not stand in for
nakahatsu.aiLimitText: There were things AI could not stand in for: design judgment, imagining the experience someone will have, and finding the format and the form that carry what matters most. The generic design AI produces will not give a first-time visitor the experience they hoped for, let alone more than that.
nakahatsu.clientLearningTitle: The design that only comes from knowing them
nakahatsu.clientLearningText: I went through the client's Instagram account and their existing site in detail to understand what they actually do. What came out of it was that this is not a shop that only sells things. They run miso and soy sauce making workshops for people of every age and background. Relationships with people are part of the business. That is where a new section on the home page came from, headed "Us and our customers", introducing that side of their work.
nakahatsu.copyTitle: The words were carried over unchanged
nakahatsu.copyText: The Japanese body copy on the site is the client's original text, carried over as it was. It is plain, serious, and sincere enough that you feel all of that from the writing alone. I wanted the design to be true to that, so I aimed for something quiet and beautiful with something firm at the centre of it. The English is Shopify's machine translation, which I revised, and the French is based on a draft from Claude. The client has not yet confirmed either.
nakahatsu.captionChallenges: From the previous site: the list of payment methods, how shipping and delivery were described, and the sign-up error.
nakahatsu.referencesNote: Ten sites in Japan that sell soy sauce, miso and other fermented foods, surveyed in the first month of the project. All are the companies' own public sites. How I chose them is described under "Survey of similar sites".
nakahatsu.captionAbout: The About page in Japanese: the miso block. The body text runs vertically over a photograph, and the heading stands vertically to its right.
nakahatsu.heroAlt: The new Nakahatsu Shoten site on a desktop and a phone: the home page hero, and a product page.
nakahatsu.aiNote: I used AI (Claude) for implementation and translation, and also for the design work in Figma. I made the early-stage designs by hand and shared them, and had AI apply the existing design system and evaluate and improve the designs against design principles and usability. The aim was to save time and to keep quality up. The English is Shopify's machine translation, which I revised. The French is based on a draft from Claude. The client has not yet reviewed either.
nakahatsu.photosTitle: No photos that do not exist
nakahatsu.photosText: The history section first held placeholder images: generic old photographs with specific captions, such as the area around Tenma-cho at the time of founding. Publishing captions for photographs that do not exist seemed risky, so I stopped showing the placeholders and the timeline. At a later meeting, because the client had few documents and photos, we decided to keep the history section simple and to use a photo of the founder. The client supplied it, and it has been placed.
nakahatsu.heritageTitle: Six long-established companies whose history pages I studied
nakahatsu.heritageNote: At the start of the second month I looked at each history page to see how the company tells its history.
nakahatsu.moodboardNote: Three options made to compare design directions.

nakahatsuSy.title: Nakahatsu Shoten Website
nakahatsuSy.overviewCatch: Making a company site and a shop into one store.
overview: Nakahatsu Shoten makes soy sauce and miso in Kanazawa. It was founded in 1896 as a food retailer and later moved into brewing.

The company site ran on WordPress and the shop on EC-CUBE, as two separate systems. I took the project on as an individual, through an introduction from an acquaintance, and handle the proposal, the design, the Shopify implementation, and display in Japanese, English and French. This phase is a domestic shop; selling overseas is outside the scope.
nakahatsuSy.processCatch: From "keep the existing design" to a design that carries Nakahatsu Shoten's strengths.
process: The first agreement was to keep the existing design and skip wireframes. After that I proposed a redesign. The reason was that, from Nakahatsu Shoten's daily posts on Instagram, I sensed a shop that welcomes people from Japan and abroad, of every age, and values its relationships with them. I wanted the site to express that strength fully, and to convey the history and the people behind it.
In the proposal I explained the reasons for the change, together with how much I respect what Nakahatsu Shoten does.

steps.h: Sorting out the state of the existing site
p: The shop could not take credit cards; the only ways to pay were bank transfer, postal transfer and cash on delivery. The site was in Japanese only, with no official translation, so a visitor who could not read Japanese had to rely on machine translation. What buyers want to know before purchase was only partly written on the legal notice page.
Because the company site and the shop were separate systems, the design and the updates were both done twice.
steps.cap: The company-introduction site and the shop ran on two systems (WordPress and EC-CUBE); they became one Shopify store.

steps.h: Showing two versions side by side
p: I made one version that reproduced the structure of the existing site in Shopify theme code (v1) and one redesign (v2), and shared them side by side. Nakahatsu Shoten replied that v2 was easy to see, with a clean structure that included the purchase path (summarised). I have worked mainly on v2 since.
steps.cap: Before: the top page of the WordPress company site. After: the new top page. The shop was a separate system (EC-CUBE).

steps.h: Reworking the home page and About page
p: In the hero section, the changes are a larger logo and a short message that continues from 天の恵み ("the blessings of heaven"). The photographs are a carousel of three images both before and after, and the three images are the same; the figure differs only in when the screenshot was taken. The header carries a language switch (Japanese, English and French) and the cart. For people who visit the site often, I moved the news from the lower part of the old site to just below the hero.
steps.cap: The About page in Japanese: the miso block. The body text runs vertically over a photograph, and the heading stands vertically to its right.

p: The site was Japanese only. It can now be read in English and French too. The contract covers Japanese and English; Nakahatsu Shoten asked for French to be added, because many visits to the site come from France.
steps.cap: The same hero in Japanese, English and French.

steps.h: The brand color, and keeping values in sync
p: The brand color is enji, a deep crimson. It is one of the Kaga Gosai, the five traditional colors of Kanazawa, and it is rooted in the culture of this place.
When the values in Figma and in code drift apart, I look at the site to fix something and find that Figma no longer matches it. So a script keeps the color and spacing values the same in both.
steps.cap: The brand's enji, and the theme colors sumi brown and washi. Each color shows its HEX, RGB and where it is used.

nakahatsuSy.statusCatch: Not yet public. No figures yet.
status: The client's site has not launched, so there are no sales or conversion figures. After launch I plan to look at unique users, sales and purchase completion, and word-of-mouth feedback. These are not metrics agreed with the client. I also hope to see more visitors from French-speaking regions.

iterFig.lead: The process section went through five forms before reaching the current ring of five circles. They are listed in time order.
groups: 1. Around Oct 12: photo and text side by side

I started with a large work photo on the left and the client's text on the right. The minutes of the Oct 6 meeting say the brewer section had too much text and felt heavy, so I would offer several layouts with large photos and white space.
2. Around Oct 14: products and logo

The logo and product images sit on the left, with a purple watercolor in the lower right. This is also the 'current' layout I showed the client. The process photos had not arrived yet (the client gathered them on Oct 25).
3. Two of the three forms I showed the client, not chosen
A places the five circles on a circle, joined by a thin line. B places them in a straight line. I showed the client these two together with the current layout.
4. Exploring the ring
To refine the ring, I looked up the Japanese plum-blossom crest (umebachi mon), gathered the five circles like that crest, and made four variations of the lines and the dot.
5. Final: a ring with lines from the center
The client chose the ring and asked to shorten its last part. I showed three options as videos, and the client liked the third, with five lines growing from a center circle. I applied it on Nov 2.

ringFig.title: Our Brewing Process
ringFig.leadText: Both the soy sauce and the miso that bear the Tenyu name ("a gift from heaven") are made without a single food additive.
rest: Adding nothing extra. Using only carefully chosen ingredients. Brewing in the oldest, most natural way possible. Since our founding, that is what we have committed to so that you can eat with peace of mind.
From preparing the grain to making kōji, mashing, fermenting, aging, pressing, and finishing: every step happens in our own brewery, under our own care.
We listen to the soy sauce and miso as they brew. We take the time that mass production cannot afford, and we keep working by hand.

nakahatsuSy.aboutText: The old About page was mostly text, with photographs sized to sit beside it. In the new About page, each section carries a photograph or a figure, placed large, that matches what the section wants to say. The brewers are shown through photographs of their work, and the ingredients through a map of where they come from, so that each point can be seen at a glance. The page can be read to the end as one story.

topIter.lead: I redesigned the About section of the home page twice. There are nine designs I did not use, in two directions. The one I used places two photographs of the building side by side.
groups: A. First round: photographs of ingredients (7 designs)
The heading is 「100年変わらない自然製法」, which means natural methods unchanged for 100 years. The designs place photographs of the ingredients and the barrel staggered, in curved bands, or cut into circles.
B. Second round: photographs of the building (2 designs)

The heading became 「中初商店について」, which means About Nakahatsu Shoten, and the photographs show the inside of the building. One design staggers four photographs; the other places three photographs at the same size.
